To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

chronic stress exposure is associated with increased connectivity within somatosensory and visual networks and with the default mode network, as well as increased lateral ventricular volume and diffusivities.
chronic stress exposure induces changes in functional connectivity patterns and in the volume of the lateral ventricle.
chronic stress exposure is associated with altered functional network connectivity strength and increased lateral ventricular volume in the rodent model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of chronic psychosocial stress on the brain and its functional connectivity patterns in rodents.
the identification of the neural mechanisms underlying the effects of stress on brain structure and function.
the effects of chronic psychological stress on large scale brain networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chronic stress-induced functional connectivity alterations observed in rodents resemble those observed in human studies.
stress-induced changes in functional connectivity are more pronounced than volumetric changes.
chronic stress exposure induces structural changes in the brain which may be related to changes in functional connectivity patterns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic stress exposure is associated with increased functional connectivity within sensory, visual, and DMN networks and increased volume and diffisivity of lateral ventricle.
chronic stress induces a pattern of functional network connectivity that is associated with a more negative emotional bias, as is seen in depression and anxiety.
chronic stress induces alterations in large-scale brain networks that are similar to those observed in stress related psychopathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stress-related alterations in brain function may be more pronounced than those in brain structure.
chronic stress induces alterations in functional connectivity of large brain networks, and that these changes are more pronounced than those in gross volumetric changes.
chronic stress induces changes in functional connectivity in large-scale brain networks, which may contribute to the development of stress-related psychopathologies.
